title: Lexing and Parsing
tagline: How raw source text becomes structured meaning — the two-stage pipeline every compiler and interpreter begins with.

sections.content:
Type `const x = 1 + 2;` into a JavaScript file and press run. Within milliseconds the engine has read those 18 characters, decided they represent a variable declaration with an arithmetic expression on the right-hand side, verified the expression is structurally valid, evaluated it to `3`, and stored the result. How does that happen? The raw source file is just a sequence of Unicode code points — a river of characters with no inherent meaning. Before any evaluation can occur, the program text must be **understood**, and understanding requires two distinct stages: **lexing** and **parsing**.

**Lexing** (also called *tokenising* or *scanning*) is the first stage. It reads the character stream left-to-right and groups characters into **tokens** — the smallest meaningful units of the language. A token is something like `KEYWORD('const')`, `IDENTIFIER('x')`, `EQUALS`, `NUMBER(1)`, `PLUS`, `NUMBER(2)`, `SEMICOLON`. Whitespace and comments are silently discarded; they separate tokens but carry no grammatical meaning in most languages. The lexer does not care about structure — it only cares about recognising atomic units.

**Parsing** is the second stage. It takes the flat token stream produced by the lexer and builds a **hierarchical tree** — the **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)** — that captures the grammatical structure of the program. The AST for `const x = 1 + 2` is a tree whose root is a `VariableDeclaration` node with a `BinaryExpression` subtree on the right side, and `Literal` leaves at the bottom. That tree is what the rest of the compiler or interpreter actually operates on.

Together, lexing and parsing form the **front-end** of every compiler, interpreter, linter, formatter, code highlighter, and transpiler ever built. JavaScript's V8, Python's CPython, Rust's `rustc`, TypeScript's language server, ESLint, Prettier, Babel — all begin with exactly this two-stage pipeline. Understanding it gives you genuine insight into why `SyntaxError` messages exist, what AST-level tooling like Babel or eslint plugins actually manipulate, how syntax highlighting works, and what the difference between a lexical error and a syntax error really is. It is also one of the most beautiful application areas of formal language theory, turning abstract grammar rules into working code.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Source Code\n(character stream)"] --> B["Lexer / Tokeniser"]
    B --> C["Token Stream"]
    C --> D["Parser"]
    D --> E["AST"]
    E --> F["Semantic Analysis"]
    F --> G["Code Generation\nor Interpretation"]
    B --> H["Lexical Error"]
    D --> I["Syntax Error"]
    H --> J["Error Reporter"]
    I --> J
sections.caption: The compiler front-end pipeline. Source text flows through lexer → token stream → parser → AST. Each stage can produce distinct error types: lexical errors come from unrecognised characters; syntax errors come from grammatically invalid token sequences.

sections.title: Reading a Sentence in a Foreign Language
sections.content:
Imagine you are studying Latin and you encounter the sentence *"Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres."* Your brain performs two very different operations as you process it.

First, you **split the stream of letters into words and punctuation**: `Gallia`, `est`, `omnis`, `divisa`, `in`, `partes`, `tres`, `.`. Each word is a discrete unit — a token. You can identify them even if you do not know the meaning yet. You also assign each a rough category: noun, verb, adjective, preposition, noun, noun, numeral, period. This is lexing. If you suddenly see `@##` in the middle of the sentence you know immediately that it does not belong — that is a **lexical error** because those characters are not part of the Latin character set.

Second, you **parse the grammatical structure**: `Gallia` is nominative (the subject), `est divisa` is the passive predicate, `omnis` modifies the subject, `in partes tres` is a prepositional phrase modifying the predicate. You build a mental tree of relationships. If you read `est Gallia divisa omnis tres partes in` — all real Latin words, none illegal — but the case endings clash and the structure is incoherent, you have a **syntax error**: valid tokens arranged in a grammatically invalid sequence.

This two-failure-mode structure maps exactly to compiler front-ends. Lexical errors arise from characters the language does not recognise. Syntax errors arise from token sequences that violate grammar rules. They are fundamentally different problems caught at different stages, which is why their error messages look different in practice.

sections.title: The Lexer in Detail — Turning Characters into Tokens
sections.content:
A **lexer** is a state machine that reads the input character by character and, according to a set of rules, decides when it has accumulated enough characters to emit a token. The rules are usually specified as **regular expressions** or a hand-written equivalent.

For a small language with the token classes `NUMBER`, `IDENT`, `KEYWORD`, `PLUS`, `MINUS`, `STAR`, `SLASH`, `EQ`, `SEMI`, and `EOF`, the lexer loops over the source string and applies rules in priority order:

1. **Skip whitespace** — spaces, tabs, newlines are consumed and ignored.
2. **Match the longest prefix** — this is the **maximal munch** rule. If the input is `==`, the lexer should emit a single `EQEQ` token, not two `EQ` tokens. It always greedily consumes as many characters as possible while still matching a valid token pattern.
3. **Classify keywords vs. identifiers** — the lexer typically recognises all alphabetic strings as identifiers first, then checks whether the matched string is in a reserved keyword set (`let`, `if`, `return`, etc.). Keywords take precedence.
4. **Attach position information** — good lexers record the `line` and `column` (or byte offset) of each token. This is what powers the `line 4, column 12` portion of error messages.
5. **Discard comments** — `// ...` or `/* ... */` are consumed and discarded just like whitespace. They are not emitted into the token stream.

Each emitted token is typically a small record: `{ type, value, line, col }`. For example, tokenising `let total = 10 + 32;` produces:

`KEYWORD(let)` `IDENT(total)` `EQ(=)` `NUMBER(10)` `PLUS(+)` `NUMBER(32)` `SEMI(;)` `EOF`

The `EOF` sentinel is crucial — it tells the parser that the input has ended, preventing off-the-end reads.

**What the lexer does NOT do**: it does not check whether `let` is being used correctly, whether `total` has been declared, or whether the expression on the right-hand side is valid. Those are parsing and semantic analysis concerns. The lexer is intentionally narrow and fast — it makes a single left-to-right pass over the character stream in O(n) time.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Start
    Start --> SkipWS: whitespace
    SkipWS --> Start: done
    Start --> InNumber: digit
    InNumber --> InNumber: digit
    InNumber --> EmitNumber: non-digit
    EmitNumber --> Start
    Start --> InWord: letter or _
    InWord --> InWord: letter, digit, _
    InWord --> EmitWord: other
    EmitWord --> Start
    Start --> EmitOp: operator char
    EmitOp --> Start
    Start --> [*]: EOF
sections.caption: A simplified lexer state machine. The lexer transitions between states as it reads characters. When it exits a token-accumulating state (InNumber, InWord), it emits the token and returns to Start.

sections.title: Formal Grammars — The Rules a Parser Enforces
sections.content:
A **grammar** is a precise specification of which token sequences are valid in a language. The most common notation is **BNF** (Backus-Naur Form) or its extended variant **EBNF**. A grammar is a collection of **production rules** of the form:

`nonterminal ::= body`

where the body is a combination of **terminal symbols** (tokens, written in uppercase or quotes) and **nonterminals** (rule names, written in lowercase or angle brackets). For example, a tiny arithmetic grammar might look like:

```
program    ::= statement* EOF
statement  ::= letDecl | exprStmt
letDecl    ::= 'let' IDENT '=' expression ';'
exprStmt   ::= expression ';'
expression ::= term (('+' | '-') term)*
term       ::= factor (('*' | '/') factor)*
factor     ::= NUMBER | IDENT | '(' expression ')'
```

Every valid program is a sequence of tokens that can be derived from the start symbol (`program`) by repeatedly expanding nonterminals according to the rules. The **parser's job** is to verify that the incoming token stream matches one of these derivations and to simultaneously build the tree that records which derivation was used.

**Why grammars matter practically**: If you want to understand why JavaScript allows `(a = b) = c` to be a parse error even though `a = b` and `b = c` are both valid — or why you cannot write `if (x) else` without a consequent branch — the answer lives in the grammar. Grammars are not just academic formalism; they are the authoritative source of truth for language syntax.

**Operator precedence** is encoded in the grammar by nesting. Notice that `factor` is nested inside `term`, which is nested inside `expression`. The deeper the rule, the higher the precedence. Multiplication `*` binds tighter than addition `+` because `*` is handled at the `term` level, closer to the leaves of the tree, before `+` is handled at the `expression` level. This is not a special case — it falls naturally out of grammar nesting.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["expression"] --> B["term"]
    A --> C["+"]
    A --> D["term"]
    B --> E["factor"]
    B --> F["*"]
    B --> G["factor"]
    E --> H["NUMBER 2"]
    G --> I["NUMBER 3"]
    D --> J["factor"]
    J --> K["NUMBER 4"]
sections.caption: Parse tree for '2 * 3 + 4'. Multiplication is deeper (higher precedence) — the subtree '2 * 3' is a child of expression, ensuring it is evaluated first, matching mathematical convention.

sections.title: Recursive Descent Parsing — Grammar Rules as Functions
sections.content:
The most readable and most commonly hand-written parsing technique is **recursive descent**. The key insight is elegant: each grammar rule becomes a function that returns an AST node.

- `parseProgram()` loops calling `parseStatement()` until EOF.
- `parseStatement()` peeks at the next token to decide which branch to call (`parseLetDecl()`, `parseIfStmt()`, `parseExprStmt()`).
- `parseExpression()` calls `parseTerm()`, then loops consuming `+` or `-` operators and calling `parseTerm()` again, building a left-associative `BinaryExpression` node.
- `parseTerm()` calls `parseFactor()`, similarly looping for `*` and `/`.
- `parseFactor()` handles `NUMBER`, `IDENT`, and parenthesised sub-expressions — and it calls `parseExpression()` for the parenthesised case, which is the **recursion** that gives the technique its name.

The call stack during parsing naturally mirrors the tree being built. When `parseTerm()` calls `parseFactor()`, the call frame on the stack corresponds to a parent-child relationship in the AST.

**Lookahead**: Recursive descent parsers typically use **one token of lookahead** (LL(1)) — they peek at the current token to decide which rule to apply without consuming it. Some grammars require more lookahead (LL(k)) or backtracking. The `peek()` operation is free since the lexer has already emitted the token.

**The `consume()` / `expect()` primitive**: Every parser function uses a helper that asserts the current token has the expected type, consumes it, and returns it. If the assertion fails, a `SyntaxError` is thrown with the current position. This is how `Unexpected token ')'` messages are generated — the parser expected a `SEMICOLON` but found `RPAREN`.

**Left recursion**: A naive recursive descent parser cannot handle left-recursive rules like `expression ::= expression '+' term | term` because the recursive call would immediately call itself again without consuming any input, causing infinite recursion. The standard fix is to rewrite the rule as an iteration (a `while` loop), as shown in the grammar above.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["parseExpression()"] --> B["parseTerm()"]
    A --> C["loop on + or -"]
    B --> D["parseFactor()"]
    B --> E["loop on * or /"]
    D --> F["NUMBER token"] 
    D --> G["IDENT token"]
    D --> H["parseFactor calls\nparseExpression for ()"]
    H --> A
sections.caption: Call structure of a recursive descent parser. Each rule is a function. The mutual recursion between parseFactor and parseExpression handles parenthesised sub-expressions and gives the parser its name.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The lexer applies the maximal munch rule (two-character `==` is checked before single-character `=`) and records line numbers for error messages. The parser maps each grammar rule to a function. Notice how `parseExpression` handles `+`/`-` in a while loop to avoid left recursion, and `parseFactor` recursively calls `parseExpression` for parenthesised sub-expressions. The tree structure directly mirrors the grammar hierarchy.

sections.title: Abstract vs. Concrete Syntax Trees
sections.content:
It is worth distinguishing two related concepts: the **Concrete Syntax Tree (CST)** and the **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)**.

A **CST** (also called a *parse tree*) is a complete record of every token and every grammar rule applied during parsing. Every leaf is a token, including parentheses, semicolons, and keywords. The tree is entirely faithful to the source text. CSTs are useful when you need round-trip fidelity (e.g., a formatter that must preserve all whitespace and comments).

An **AST** is a simplified, semantically meaningful tree. Syntactic noise is dropped. Parentheses do not appear as nodes — they are implied by the tree structure itself (a child node is by definition inside its parent). Semicolons are dropped. Keywords like `let` are implied by the node type (`LetDeclaration`). The AST captures *what the program means*, not *exactly how it was spelled*.

For most downstream uses — type checking, code generation, linting, optimisation — the AST is the right representation. The **ESTree** specification (used by Babel, acorn, ESLint) is the de facto standard AST format for JavaScript. TypeScript has its own AST exposed via the compiler API. Python exposes its AST through the built-in `ast` module.

**Why this matters for tooling**: When you write an ESLint rule, a Babel transform, or a TypeScript language server plugin, you are writing a **tree visitor** — a function that walks AST nodes. You are not parsing; someone else did that already. The pattern is: call the parser once, get a tree, then walk the tree applying your analysis or transformation logic. This is the architecture of every major JS ecosystem tool.

flowchart TD
    A["LetDeclaration\nname: total"] --> B["BinaryExpr\nop: +"]
    B --> C["Literal\nvalue: 10"]
    B --> D["Literal\nvalue: 32"]
    A2["Concrete Parse Tree"] --> B2["KEYWORD let"]
    A2 --> C2["IDENT total"]
    A2 --> D2["EQ ="]
    A2 --> E2["NUMBER 10"]
    A2 --> F2["PLUS +"]
    A2 --> G2["NUMBER 32"]
    A2 --> H2["SEMI ;"]
    style A fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style B fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style D fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
sections.caption: Left (green): the AST for 'let total = 10 + 32' — only semantically meaningful nodes. Right: the full concrete parse tree — every token preserved as a leaf. The AST discards punctuation whose meaning is captured by tree structure.

sections.title: Error Handling — Lexical Errors, Syntax Errors, and Recovery
sections.content:
Understanding the **taxonomy of errors** the front-end produces clarifies countless error messages you encounter every day.

**Lexical errors** occur when the lexer encounters a character (or sequence of characters) that cannot be the start of any valid token. Examples:
- `let x = @42;` — `@` is not a valid token start in most languages → `Unexpected character '@'`
- `let x = 0x9G;` — the hex literal `0x9G` is malformed because `G` is not a hex digit
- A string literal that opens with `"` but never closes → `Unterminated string literal`

The fix is always in the source text at or near the flagged position — the program has characters that are simply not part of the language's alphabet.

**Syntax errors** occur when the lexer produces valid tokens but they appear in an order that violates grammar rules. Examples:
- `let = x 5;` — all tokens are valid individually, but `=` cannot follow `let` without an identifier first
- `if (x` — the `RPAREN` that closes the condition is missing
- `function ()` — anonymous function declarations require a name in some contexts

The fix requires rearranging or adding tokens — the error is structural, not character-level.

**Semantic errors** (not caught by the parser) occur when the AST is structurally valid but semantically wrong:
- `let x = y + 1;` where `y` was never declared → `ReferenceError` / `Cannot find name 'y'`
- `let x: number = 'hello';` in TypeScript → type mismatch

These require knowledge of *meaning* (what variables are in scope, what types are assigned) that the grammar does not encode.

**Error recovery**: A production-quality parser does not stop at the first syntax error. It tries to *synchronise* — it skips tokens or inserts synthetic placeholders to get back to a known-good state (typically the start of the next statement) and continues parsing. This is why TypeScript's compiler can report ten errors at once. Common recovery strategies include:
- **Panic mode**: skip tokens until a synchronisation point (`;`, `}`, keyword) is found
- **Phrase-level recovery**: insert or delete single tokens to fix common mistakes (e.g., inserting a missing `)`)
- **Error productions**: explicitly add grammar rules for common mistakes and emit specialised error messages

Good error messages are an art form. The difference between `SyntaxError: Unexpected token ')'` and `Expected ';' after variable declaration` is enormous from a developer experience standpoint.

The full pipeline — lex → parse → evaluate — is demonstrated end-to-end. The comments show equivalent real-world usage via @babel/parser (JavaScript) and Python's built-in ast module.

sections.title: Operator Precedence and Associativity — How Grammars Encode Math
sections.content:
One of the most elegant aspects of recursive descent parsing is how **operator precedence** falls out automatically from grammar nesting, with no special-case logic required.

Consider `2 + 3 * 4`. Mathematics says the answer is 14, not 20, because `*` has higher precedence than `+`. How does the parser know this?

Because `parseTerm()` (which handles `*`) is called *from within* `parseExpression()` (which handles `+`). When `parseExpression()` calls `parseTerm()`, the entire multiplication subtree `3 * 4` is parsed and returned as a single node before `parseExpression()` sees the `+`. The tree naturally places `*` deeper (closer to leaves) than `+`, which means `*` binds its operands tighter.

**Associativity** — whether `1 - 2 - 3` means `(1 - 2) - 3` (left-associative, correct) or `1 - (2 - 3)` (right-associative, incorrect for subtraction) — is determined by the direction of the loop in the parsing function.

- **Left-associative** (most operators: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`): Use a `while` loop that accumulates the left side, producing a left-leaning tree.
- **Right-associative** (exponentiation `**`, assignment `=`): Use right-recursion — the right-hand side is parsed by a recursive call to the *same* level function, producing a right-leaning tree.

For example, `a = b = c` in JavaScript means `a = (b = c)` — assignment is right-associative. This is encoded by calling `parseAssignment()` recursively on the right side rather than looping.

Most language specifications list operator precedence tables (JavaScript has 20 levels from comma to grouping). Each level in the table corresponds to one parsing function in a recursive descent parser. This direct correspondence between the formal specification and the implementation code is what makes recursive descent so appealing for hand-written parsers.

sections.title: Beyond Recursive Descent — Other Parsing Strategies
sections.content:
Recursive descent (LL parsing) is not the only game in town. A brief survey of alternatives gives important context.

**Pratt Parsing (Top-Down Operator Precedence)**: Invented by Vaughan Pratt in 1973, this technique handles operator precedence through *binding power* numbers attached to each token type rather than through grammar nesting. Each token has a left-binding power (how tightly it binds to the expression on its left) and a right-binding power (how tightly it binds to the right). The algorithm is elegant and handles complex precedence hierarchies — including mixfix operators and user-defined operators — more cleanly than layered recursive descent. Douglas Crockford's `JSLint` parser and many modern interpreter implementations use Pratt parsing for expressions while using recursive descent for statements.

**LR Parsing (Bottom-Up)**: LR parsers read tokens and *shift* them onto a stack, then *reduce* a matched sequence of stack items to a nonterminal according to a grammar rule. The decisions are driven by a precomputed table derived from the grammar. LR parsers can handle a wider class of grammars than LL parsers (LR(k) strictly contains LL(k)) and are used by parser generators like **Yacc**, **Bison**, and **LALR** tools. The tradeoff: LR parsers are difficult to write by hand; you typically describe the grammar in a DSL and generate the parser automatically.

**Parser Generators**: Tools like **ANTLR** (Java/multiple targets), **PEG.js** / **nearley** (JavaScript), and **Lark** (Python) take a grammar description and produce a working parser automatically. You write the grammar; the tool generates the code. This is valuable for complex languages where maintaining a hand-written parser would be error-prone.

**PEG (Parsing Expression Grammars)**: An alternative formalism where alternation is *ordered* (first match wins, not ambiguous). PEGs naturally express the maximal munch rule and are never ambiguous. They can express some constructs that CFGs cannot (like indentation-sensitive syntax). `pest` (Rust) and `PEG.js` use this formalism.

**In practice**: For production compilers of widely-used languages, hand-written recursive descent is the norm. V8 (JavaScript), TypeScript, CPython, Clang (C/C++), Go, and Rust all use hand-written recursive descent parsers. The control and quality of error messages that a hand-written parser enables outweighs the automation benefits of parser generators at language-compiler scale.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Grammar Description"] --> B["Parser Generator\nANTLR / Bison / PEG.js"]
    B --> C["Generated Parser Code"]
    D["Hand-written\nRecursive Descent"] --> E["Parser Code\ndirectly authored"]
    C --> F["Token Stream"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["AST"]
sections.caption: Two routes to a parser: use a parser generator (specify grammar, get code) or hand-write a recursive descent parser. Production compilers for major languages almost universally choose the hand-written route for control and error quality.

sections.title: Real-World Applications — Lexing and Parsing in the Wild
sections.content:
The lexer-parser pipeline is far more pervasive than just compilers. Any time a program reads structured text, it is almost certainly doing some form of lexing and parsing.

**Syntax highlighting**: Your editor tokenises the source file continuously as you type. Token types are mapped to colours. The lexer runs incrementally — only re-tokenising changed regions — so highlighting updates feel instant even in large files. The parser may run asynchronously to provide bracket matching and code folding.

**Linters and formatters**: ESLint calls `@babel/parser` or `acorn` to get an AST, then walks the tree applying rule checkers at each node type. Prettier parses your code into an AST, discards all formatting, then reprints the AST through its own layout algorithm. The key insight: **formatting is a property of the AST, not the source text**.

**Transpilers**: Babel takes JavaScript source, produces an AST, applies plugins that transform AST nodes (e.g., converting ES2022 syntax to ES5), then reprints the transformed AST back to JavaScript. TypeScript's compiler does the same, additionally type-checking between the parse and emit phases.

**Database query engines**: SQL is a language. Before executing `SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 30`, the database lexes it into tokens (`SELECT`, `name`, `FROM`, `users`, `WHERE`, `age`, `>`, `30`) and parses them into a query AST. The query planner then optimises the AST before generating an execution plan.

**JSON parsing**: Even `JSON.parse('{ "x": 42 }')` is lexing and parsing — the input is tokenised into `LBRACE`, `STRING(x)`, `COLON`, `NUMBER(42)`, `RBRACE`, then parsed into a JavaScript object tree.

**Template engines**: Mustache, Handlebars, Jinja — all lex the template string to find `{{` and `}}` delimiters, then parse the expressions inside. The template AST is then evaluated against a data context.

**Domain-specific languages (DSLs)**: Configuration files (TOML, YAML), regular expression engines, CSS selectors, GraphQL queries, Markdown — all involve lexing and parsing. When you write a complex CSS selector like `div.container > p:first-child`, a CSS engine lexes and parses it into a selector tree before applying it to the DOM.

Understanding this pipeline means you understand the foundation of an enormous surface area of modern software. Writing even a small toy parser — for a calculator, a config file, a tiny scripting language — is one of the most illuminating programming exercises you can undertake.

**Historical context**: Formal grammars were introduced by Noam Chomsky in 1956 as a model of natural language. John Backus adapted the notation for the ALGOL 60 programming language specification in 1959, creating what we now call BNF. The first fully automatic compiler front-end was built for FORTRAN by John Backus's team at IBM (1954-1957). Recursive descent parsing was formalised by Peter Lucas and others in the early 1960s. YACC (Yet Another Compiler Compiler), which popularised LR parsing for practical language implementation, was written by Stephen Johnson at Bell Labs in 1970. The tools have evolved but the core ideas — tokenise, build a grammar, derive a tree — are unchanged after 65 years.

**Common misconceptions and interview traps**: First, lexical errors and syntax errors are distinct — do not confuse them. A `@` character is a *lexical* error; `let = x 5` is a *syntax* error. Second, the parser does NOT check whether variables are declared or types match — that is semantic analysis, the next stage. Third, operator precedence is encoded in grammar nesting, not in special parser logic — each precedence level is one function. Fourth, whitespace discarding is a *lexer* responsibility, not the parser's. Fifth, real-world parsers use one-token lookahead (LL(1)) for most decisions — if you find yourself needing many tokens of lookahead, it usually signals a grammar design problem. Sixth, for production JavaScript or TypeScript work, never write your own parser — use `@babel/parser`, `acorn`, or the TypeScript compiler API; they handle every edge case in the specification that would take months to get right.

items: **Lexing** converts a raw character stream into a flat sequence of typed **tokens** by applying regular expression patterns (or equivalent state machines) left-to-right, discarding whitespace and comments; it runs in O(n) time.
**Parsing** converts the token stream into a hierarchical **AST** by applying grammar rules; the tree structure encodes grammatical relationships and drives all subsequent compiler/tool stages.

**Lexical errors** arise when a character cannot start any valid token; **syntax errors** arise when valid tokens appear in a grammatically invalid order; **semantic errors** (undeclared variables, type mismatches) are a third, distinct category caught only after the AST is built.

**Recursive descent parsing** maps each grammar production rule directly to a function; operator precedence falls naturally from grammar nesting, and associativity from whether the function loops (left-associative) or recurses (right-associative).
**Grammars** written in BNF/EBNF are the authoritative specification of language syntax; every SyntaxError you have ever seen corresponds to a grammar rule violation at a specific token position.

The **AST** is the lingua franca of language tooling — ESLint rules, Babel transforms, TypeScript plugins, formatters, and minifiers all work by walking and transforming AST nodes, never raw source text.

This two-stage pipeline appears in SQL engines, template languages, configuration parsers, syntax highlighters, and DSLs — any tool that reads structured text is doing lexing and parsing in some form.

quiz.question: What is the primary output of the lexing (tokenising) stage?
options: An Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
Machine code ready for execution
A flat stream of typed tokens
A control-flow graph
quiz.explanation: The lexer converts the raw character stream into a sequence of typed tokens (e.g. KEYWORD, IDENT, NUMBER). The AST is produced by the parser in the next stage.

quiz.question: A file contains the character `@` which is not defined in the language's token rules. What kind of error does this produce?
options: Runtime error
Semantic error
Syntax error
Lexical error
quiz.explanation: An unrecognised character that cannot be matched to any token pattern is a lexical (scanner) error, caught in the lexing stage before parsing begins.

quiz.question: In recursive descent parsing, what does each grammar rule map to?
options: A regular expression
A function that parses that rule
A database table row
A token type constant
quiz.explanation: Recursive descent parsers implement each grammar production as a function (e.g. parseExpression(), parseStatement()). The call hierarchy mirrors the grammar hierarchy, and mutual recursion handles nested constructs.

quiz.question: Why does operator precedence fall out automatically from a layered recursive descent grammar, with no special-case precedence table needed?
options: The parser reads tokens in reverse order for high-precedence operators
Higher-precedence operators are parsed at deeper grammar levels, closer to leaf nodes
The lexer attaches precedence metadata to each operator token
The AST is rewritten after parsing using a separate precedence climber
quiz.explanation: In a layered grammar, multiplication is handled inside parseTerm(), which is called by parseExpression() for addition. Deeper nesting means tighter binding. The tree naturally places * subtrees as children of + nodes, ensuring correct evaluation order.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a syntax (parse) error, as opposed to a lexical error?
options: A character like `$` appears that is not part of the token alphabet
A number literal `0x9G` is malformed
Tokens are all valid but arranged in an order that violates the grammar
The source file uses an unexpected byte-order mark
quiz.explanation: A syntax error occurs when individually valid tokens appear in an order that violates grammar rules (e.g. `= let x 5`). Options A, B, and D are lexical or pre-lexical problems caught before the parser runs.

quiz.question: What is the 'maximal munch' rule in lexing?
options: Always prefer the shortest token that matches
Always greedily consume as many characters as possible while still matching a valid token
Consume all remaining characters until end of line
Match tokens using the most recently defined rule
quiz.explanation: Maximal munch means the lexer greedily matches the longest possible token. This is why `==` is emitted as a single EQEQ token rather than two EQ tokens, and why `<=` is one token rather than LT + EQ.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and a Concrete Syntax Tree (CST)?
options: An AST is built by the lexer; a CST is built by the parser
An AST drops syntactic noise like parentheses and semicolons; a CST preserves every token as a leaf
An AST can only represent expressions; a CST represents full programs
An AST is used only in interpreted languages; a CST is used only in compiled languages
quiz.explanation: A CST preserves every token from the source, including punctuation whose meaning is captured by tree structure. An AST is simplified — parentheses are implied by the tree hierarchy, semicolons and keywords are implicit in node types. The AST is what compiler back-ends and tools operate on.

quiz.question: What does 'error recovery' mean in the context of parsing?
options: The parser restarts from the beginning of the file after each error
The parser skips or inserts tokens to resynchronise and continue reporting further errors
The lexer re-tokenises the error region with relaxed rules
The AST is patched by semantic analysis to remove invalid nodes
quiz.explanation: Error recovery lets a production parser continue past the first syntax error by skipping tokens to a synchronisation point (like ';' or '}') or inserting synthetic tokens. This allows reporting multiple errors in one pass, which is why TypeScript and ESLint can list many problems at once.

quiz.question: Which of the following errors is caught by semantic analysis, NOT by the lexer or parser?
options: Missing closing parenthesis in `if (x`
Unrecognised character `#` in a language where `#` is not defined
Using a variable `y` that was never declared: `let x = y + 1`
Token sequence `let = x` where `=` appears before the identifier
quiz.explanation: Using an undeclared variable produces a valid token stream and a structurally valid AST — the grammar allows `IDENT` in expression position. Only semantic analysis, which resolves scope and checks declarations, can detect that `y` is undefined.

quiz.question: How is left-associativity (e.g. `1 - 2 - 3` meaning `(1 - 2) - 3`) encoded in a recursive descent parser?
options: By reversing the token stream before parsing
By using a while loop that accumulates the left operand, building a left-leaning tree
By calling the same parse function recursively on the left operand
By reading operators right-to-left using a stack
quiz.explanation: Left-associativity is implemented as a while loop: parse the left operand once, then loop consuming operators and new right operands, wrapping each new right operand with the accumulated left into a BinaryExpr. This produces a left-leaning tree. Right-associativity would use recursion on the right side instead.
